extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political science, history, and political economy (19th-century US institutions)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify the conditions, features, and risks that determine the durability of republican institutions and the commercial/naval destiny of the United States, as discussed in a 19th-century political analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republic more permanent than the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union is accidental—The Republican institutions have more prospect of permanence—A republic for the present the natural state of the Anglo-Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To destroy the republic 'all the laws must be changed at the same time, and a great alteration take place in manners.' The Union exists principally in the law which formed it; one revolution or change in public opinion might destroy it, but the republic has a much deeper foundation to rest upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and features of the American republican government
rubrics_metrics.description: A republican government is the slow and quiet action of society upon itself, a regular state founded upon the enlightened will of the people; a conciliatory government in which resolutions are allowed time to ripen and are discussed and executed with mature judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republican features include high value placed on morality, respect for religious belief, acknowledgment of rights, and the tranquil rule of the majority after deliberation. These qualities make the form easy to live under and help insure its duration, even if practical results are sometimes lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on majority power
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the majority is not of itself unlimited; in the moral world humanity, justice, and reason enjoy an undisputed supremacy; in the political world vested rights are treated with no less deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority recognizes two barriers—moral principles (humanity, justice) and vested rights—and if it oversteps them it is due to passions. Good republican practice requires recognizing and respecting these barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography and settlement favor municipal government
rubrics_metrics.description: It was impossible at the foundation of the States, and it would still be difficult, to establish a central administration in America: the inhabitants are dispersed over too great a space and separated by too many natural obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: America is pre-eminently the country of provincial and municipal government. The manner of colonial settlement (separate small communities) and English municipal traditions made municipal and provincial liberty deeply rooted in laws and manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional entrenchment required to overturn republicanism
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the mass of the institutions of the country is essentially republican; and in order permanently to destroy the laws which form the basis of the republic, it would be necessary to abolish all the laws at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before republican legislation can be altered the whole community must undergo very serious changes in opinions, manners, and laws; therefore dismantling republican institutions requires a broad, sustained social transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of legislative instability
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of instability: (1) that which modifies secondary laws and is compatible with a settled society; (2) that which shakes the foundations of the Constitution and attacks fundamental principles—this leads to revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows these forms can be independent; the United States commonly experiences the first kind (frequent changes to secondary laws) but not the second (attacks on constitutional foundations). Distinguishing them is crucial to assessing political stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of rapid transition from republic to despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: If republican principles are lost in America, they will speedily arrive at a despotic government without a long interval of limited monarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu observed that authority of a prince immediately succeeding a republic is often most absolute. Democratic republics that lose republican habits may transfer broad powers to a single sovereign; magistrates accustomed to wide discretionary powers may retain them under a new regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy unlikely to arise voluntarily
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocratic body is composed of citizens permanently stationed above the mass and requires the inequality of men as a fundamental principle; it cannot be created by a people by free will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical aristocracies arose by conquest or force; in a people that began democratic, establishing aristocratic, inviolable privileges would be novel and would require constraint—therefore America is unlikely to create an aristocracy from within.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and intellectual causes drive commercial superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial superiority of the Anglo-Americans is less attributable to physical circumstances than to moral and intellectual causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical advantages (coasts, ports) matter, but the author's view is that qualities like enterprise, willingness to take risks, adaptability, and general capacity of laborers explain why American shipping can be cheaper and faster than competitors'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-taking and seamanship practices as commercial advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: American merchants and sailors undertake voyages with fewer precautions (weigh anchor in gales, sail by night, repair at sea) and make fewer port calls, enabling faster voyages and lower costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'heroism' of trading yields speed (shorter voyage times) at the cost of higher risk (shipwrecks, harder life). The operational practices—minimal stops, continuous sailing, rapid turnaround—are offered as concrete practices producing lower freight rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalist economy and fluid occupations foster innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans change occupations readily, often being acquainted with many trades; lack of extreme division of labor enlarges general capacity and intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individuals may be barristers, farmers, merchants, ministers, and physicians in turn, they are not fettered by professional axioms and adopt novel methods readily. This fluidity promotes improvisation, experimentation, and commercial agility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual change and social mobility invigorate enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual change, vicissitudes of fortune, and frequent legislative change keep citizens in 'a perpetual state of feverish agitation' and make them enterprising, fond of adventure, and innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The national temperament—restless, novelty-seeking, inclined to improvement—translates into commercial daring and rapid expansion of shipping and trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval force prerequisite for durable commercial prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: No commercial prosperity can be durable if it cannot be united, in case of need, to naval force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The truth is well understood in the United States; commercial states must be willing to make sacrifices to protect shipping. Without a supporting naval power, commercial dominance cannot be securely maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic contiguity preserves maritime power despite political disunion
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissolution of the Union would not check the maritime vigor of the States; commercial states are contiguous, share opinions and interests, and would form a maritime power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if political union dissolves, commercial necessity and cheapness will bind the commercial states together for maritime enterprise; national prejudice cannot easily overcome the sovereign law of commerce—cheapness.
